# Summary of Information About Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish computer engineer and inventor born in Turin, Italy, to a family of intellectuals and mountaineers. During WWII, he was active in the Polish resistance and survived severe injuries. After the war, he excelled academically, graduating from the Warsaw University of Technology, and faced political challenges due to his Home Army past. His pioneering work included constructing the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics, 1957) and the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer, AKAT-1 (1959). He developed one of the earliest perceptrons in the communist bloc (1964), as well as the KAR-65 computer (completed in 1968), which was Poland's fastest computer at the time.
Karpiński led the development of the innovative K-202 minicomputer (early 1970s), notable for its modularity, use of Intel 4004 microchips, and advanced features like memory segmentation with paging. Despite its technical superiority over contemporaries like the PDP-11, only about 30 units were produced due to political, economic, and organizational obstacles, including opposition from competing manufacturers and lack of political support. Following disillusionment, he left the field in the late 1970s, later worked in Switzerland, and returned to Poland in the 1990s.
Controversially, Karpiński was a secret informant for the Polish security service (Służba Bezpieczeństwa) from 1961, providing technological intelligence mainly on U.S. advances, though cooperation waned as he became a target of surveillance himself. His legacy remains debated; some hail him as a visionary thwarted by the system, while others note exaggerations and challenges in his projects. He was posthumously honored with the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2010.
